units.title: Step time, token throughput and MFU versus HFU
outcomes: Define step time, tokens per second, MFU and HFU, stating the FLOP count and peak each ratio uses.
Derive tokens per second from step time and batch tokens, and MFU from model FLOPs over peak throughput.
Measure step time and tokens per second with warmup and synchronization, and label CPU timings as non-evidence for GPU interconnects.
units.why: Throughput numbers mean nothing without fixed workload semantics and stated FLOP counts. This unit fixes the definitions before any diagnosis.

next.note: Label the compute, memory or communication bound behind the throughput.
Extend single-rank throughput to scaling efficiency and failure-adjusted goodput.

study.title: MFU versus HFU and FLOP counting
study.locator: MFU vs HFU section with \(\text{HFU} = \text{actual FLOPs} / \text{peak}\) and the `FlopCounterMode` snippet; MFU is a very rough approximation subsection

study.title: Rooflines and the H100 crossover
study.locator: Where Does the Time Go through A Few Problems to Work, with Q1 on intensity and Q5 on the H100 SXM crossover near 295, with answers
study.depth: Keep TPU ICI numbers labeled as TPU numbers. Re-parameterize the crossover for your hardware before quoting it.

study.title: Roofline diagnosis and the MFU definition
study.locator: The Memory Wall and Roofline Diagnosis with the iron law and ridge table, and Measurement at Scale with the MFU bands (40 to 60 percent good, above 60 excellent)

focus: Step time is wall-clock per optimizer step at fixed global batch, sequence length and precision. Tokens per second is global-batch tokens divided by step time.
MFU uses model FLOPs, commonly \(6 N D\) for training, over peak. HFU uses actual FLOPs including recomputation and padding. State both before comparing.
MFU is rough under mixed precision because regions run in different formats while the peak assumes one. Compare before and after on the same setup, never across clusters.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive tokens per second and MFU for \(N = 10^9\) parameters, \(D = 10^6\) tokens and \(T_{\text{step}} = 30\) s at peak \(989\) TFLOP/s: tokens/s is about 33,333, model FLOPs are \(6 \times 10^{15}\), achieved about 200 TFLOP/s, MFU about 20 percent.
traps: Comparing MFUs built from different FLOP counts (with versus without attention terms, forward-only versus training) or different peaks (sparse versus dense, BF16 versus FP16).
Reading CPU `gloo` step times as evidence about GPU throughput or interconnects. They check semantics only.
Treating `FlopCounterMode` as exact. It has performance and memory problems and serves as a cross-check, not the answer.

selfTest.q: How are step time, global-batch tokens and tokens per second related?
selfTest.a: Tokens per second is \(D_{\text{tokens}} / T_{\text{step}}\) at fixed batch, sequence and precision. Change any of the three and the ratio is incomparable.

selfTest.q: Why can HFU exceed MFU on the same run?
selfTest.a: HFU counts actual FLOPs including recomputation, padding and synchronization overhead. MFU counts model FLOPs only, so extra work raises HFU but not MFU.

selfTest.q: A paper reports 55.2 percent MFU on 12,288 GPUs. Can you compare your single-GPU MFU to it?
selfTest.a: No. Different hardware, FLOP-count convention and workload. The 55.2 percent figure is MegaScale's own cluster result for a 175B model, not a transferable target.

selfTest.q: Manual arithmetic and `FlopCounterMode` disagree. Which do you trust?
selfTest.a: The manual count with stated assumptions. The counter is a cross-check with known performance and memory issues.

units.title: Strong and weak scaling efficiency and goodput under failures
outcomes: Define strong scaling, weak scaling and parallel efficiency, stating the fixed quantity in each.
Derive goodput with failures, retries and unusable work for one job size from failure rate and restart cost.
Explain why high device utilization can coexist with poor useful throughput.
units.why: More ranks can raise utilization while lowering useful output once failures, restarts and stragglers dominate. This unit separates busy hardware from finished work.

next.note: Convert goodput into cost per useful token.
Turn failure math into health checks, canaries and runbooks.

study.title: Scheduling, fragmentation and utilization grades
study.locator: The Scheduling Problem with gang scheduling and fragmentation math, and Debugging Cluster Utilization with allocated versus productive utilization

study.title: MegaScale scaling and straggler evidence
study.locator: arXiv:2402.15627v1, Sections 4 to 6: heartbeat fault loop, straggler mitigation and 55.2 percent MFU on 12,288 GPUs for a 175B model
study.depth: Treat the MFU and speedup as that cluster's results. Reproduce the method, not the numbers.

study.title: Failure taxonomy and MTTF versus job size
study.locator: arXiv:2410.21680v2, Sections 2 and 5: RSC cluster design, failure taxonomy and MTTF analysis with scheduler-side requeue metrics
study.depth: Model goodput for one job size only. Do not merge these research-cluster numbers with Llama 3 production counts.

focus: Strong scaling fixes the global problem and grows ranks. Weak scaling grows the problem with ranks, usually tokens per GPU. Efficiency is speedup over ranks, or throughput over ranks versus the baseline.
Goodput discounts failed, repeated and unusable work: restarts, preemption, straggler idle and checkpoint overhead. Busy GPUs doing repeated work raise utilization but not goodput.
Failure rate grows with job size, so large jobs pay more checkpoint and restart tax. Every MTTF number is cluster-specific.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, compute strong-scaling efficiency for \(T_1 = 100\) ms and \(T_4 = 30\) ms: speedup \(100/30 \approx 3.33\), efficiency \(3.33/4 \approx 83\) percent. Then state goodput at 90 percent effective time as \(0.9\) times raw throughput.
traps: Quoting weak-scaling efficiency without stating what is held fixed per rank (tokens, batch or model shard).
Merging interruption counts across studies. Llama 3 Table 5 and the Meta reliability MTTF come from different clusters and mixes.
Treating device utilization as useful throughput when restarts, retries and straggler idle consume the hours.

selfTest.q: What is fixed in strong scaling versus weak scaling?
selfTest.a: Strong scaling fixes the global problem size. Weak scaling grows it with ranks, typically holding tokens or work per rank fixed.

selfTest.q: Four ranks cut step time from 100 ms to 30 ms. What are speedup and efficiency?
selfTest.a: Speedup \(100/30 \approx 3.33\). Efficiency \(3.33/4 \approx 83\) percent against the single-rank baseline.

selfTest.q: How can utilization read 90 percent while goodput is poor?
selfTest.a: GPUs stay busy on repeated, failed or unusable work: restarts after interruptions, straggler waiting, and checkpoint overhead all count as utilized but not useful.

selfTest.q: Why does MTTF fall as job size grows, and what follows for checkpointing?
selfTest.a: More components mean more chances per hour that one fails. Larger jobs need cheaper checkpoints and faster restart because interruptions arrive sooner.

study.title: Continuous benchmarking and logging
study.locator: Chapter 13, Continuous Integration and Performance Benchmarking, with the HUD performance dashboard and MLPerf logging sections

focus: A fixed workload names model, data, global batch, sequence, precision and a correctness check. The Ultra-Scale heatmaps compare configs at one fixed 1M-token workload, never across workloads.
Warmup settles compilation, allocator and cache state. `torch.cuda.synchronize` and a cross-rank barrier separate launch from work. Report raw samples with median and spread from repeated trials.
A manifest records workload hash, config, code version, hardware, backend, environment flags and raw samples. The correctness guard runs with every timing so a fast wrong result fails.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, write a benchmark harness for a tiny MLP step that warms up, synchronizes with `torch.cuda.synchronize`, times repeated trials, reports median and spread, and checks the result against a single-process reference within tolerance.
traps: Timing CUDA work without synchronization. Asynchronous launch returns early and measures queueing, not execution.
Reporting one trial or a mean without warmup. Compilation, allocator growth and cache state dominate the first steps.
Changing batch, precision or data between runs and calling the difference a speedup. Fix the workload first.

selfTest.q: Why must the workload stay fixed across a comparison?
selfTest.a: Step time, tokens/s and MFU all depend on model, batch, sequence and precision. Changing any of them changes the work, so the comparison measures a different job.

selfTest.q: What goes wrong when CUDA timing omits synchronization?
selfTest.a: Kernel launches are asynchronous, so the timer stops at enqueue time. The measured time is launch overhead, far below execution time.

selfTest.q: What does warmup settle, and what happens without it?
selfTest.a: Compilation, allocator blocks and cache state. Without warmup the first trials are slower and more variable, and the mean misleads.

selfTest.q: What belongs in a regression evidence manifest?
selfTest.a: Workload identity and hash, configuration, code version, hardware and topology, backend, environment flags, raw timing samples, and the correctness-guard result.

study.title: Systematic profiling and fleet traces
study.locator: System Profiling with the drill from application to operation, and Measurement at Scale on fleet traces and gray stragglers

focus: Split the step into input wait, host transfer, forward and backward kernels, bucket collectives, optimizer and checkpoint. `torch.cuda.nvtx.range_push` and `range_pop` name regions so kernels map to source.
Ranks have skewed clocks, so align by collective entry and exit markers and sequence numbers, never by raw wall-clock order.
The profiler perturbs the run: it can disable fusion and inflate traffic. Compare with and without profiling and state the overhead beside every trace claim.
units.reproduce: Without notes, capture a three-step CPU trace with `torch.profiler.profile`, `record_shapes=True` and NVTX ranges around forward and backward, export the chrome trace, and name the top operation class by time.
traps: Ordering cross-rank events by unsynchronized wall-clock. Clock skew exceeds collective latency, so apparent order is not causal order.
Quoting profiler-inflated memory traffic as hardware truth. Fusion disabled under observation raises HBM passes the real run avoids.
Blaming the network for an NCCL wait when the peer is stalled in the data loader. The waiter is the victim; the straggler is the cause.

selfTest.q: What do NVTX ranges add to a profiler trace?
selfTest.a: Named source regions around forward, backward and transfers. Kernels inside a range inherit its label, so time maps to code instead of anonymous kernels.

selfTest.q: How do you align two rank timelines?
selfTest.a: By shared collective markers with matching sequence numbers and entry or exit events. Raw timestamps cannot order across skewed clocks.

selfTest.q: How do you check profiler overhead?
selfTest.a: Compare step time and key counters with and without the profiler on the same fixed workload. Report the difference beside trace-derived numbers.

selfTest.q: Rank 0 waits in `all_reduce` while rank 1 loads data. Which is the cause?
selfTest.a: Rank 1 input stall is the cause. Rank 0 wait is the victim symptom; fixing the network would not move the step.

units.why: A hung job parks every rank inside the same collective wait. The desync report and recorder history name the rank that never arrived.

study.locator: Enabling Flight Recorder through Analyzing Flight Recorder Dumps, with `TORCH_NCCL_TRACE_BUFFER_SIZE`, `TORCH_NCCL_DUMP_ON_TIMEOUT` and `TORCH_FR_DUMP_TEMP_FILE` (page read 2026-10-14)

study.title: Hangs with TorchComms and the debug server
study.locator: The Scenario through Running the FR CLI on Per-Rank Pickle Dumps, with `TEST_BACKEND=gloo` and `TEST_DEVICE=cpu` (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: The CPU gloo path is stated but not exercised in this unit. Treat dump reading as the exercised skill, not dump collection on CPU.

study.title: Desync reports, recorder traces and NCCL transport logs
study.locator: Diagnosing crashes hangs and tracing execution: The desync report with `TORCH_NCCL_DESYNC_DEBUG`, The flight recorder trace with `TORCH_FR_BUFFER_SIZE` and `TORCH_FR_DUMP_TEMP_FILE`, and `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO` with `NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS`

focus: The desync report names the rank and collective that fell out of step at timeout. The recorder adds per-rank collective history with Python stacks. Enable both before launching; dumps are post-mortem.

The `fr_trace` analysis aggregates per-rank pickles and shows states and sequence numbers. A collective with matching `collective_seq_id` across ranks but a missing rank points at the rank that never arrived.

`TORCH_FR_BUFFER_SIZE` and `TORCH_NCCL_DUMP_ON_TIMEOUT` are PyTorch recorder controls. `NCCL_DEBUG` and `NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS` are NCCL transport controls. Before PyTorch 2.9 the buffer variables carried `TORCH_NCCL_` names that still work with a warning.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, list the three variables that arm dump-on-timeout and the analysis command: `TORCH_FR_BUFFER_SIZE=2000`, `TORCH_NCCL_DUMP_ON_TIMEOUT=1`, `TORCH_FR_DUMP_TEMP_FILE=/tmp/fr`, then `python -m torch.distributed.flight_recorder.fr_trace` on the dump directory.
traps: Mixing recorder and transport layers. `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO` shows devices and sockets, not which Python collective mismatched.
Using the pre-2.9 buffer names without knowing they warn. Old and new names both arm the recorder, but only the new names are quiet.
Expecting NCCL flight dumps from CPU-only ranks. Collection is NCCL-gated, so on CPU read provided dumps instead of claiming local collection.

selfTest.q: What does the desync report add over a bare timeout?
selfTest.a: It names which collective and which rank fell out of step, instead of leaving every rank parked in the same wait with no attribution.

selfTest.q: The aggregated dump shows a collective with `missing_ranks` holding one rank. What does that mean?
selfTest.a: That rank never reached the collective with the matching sequence number. It is the first suspect; the waiting ranks are victims.

selfTest.q: Which controls belong to PyTorch and which to NCCL?
selfTest.a: PyTorch owns the recorder buffer, dump-on-timeout and dump path. NCCL owns `NCCL_DEBUG`, `NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS`, interface selection and transport logging.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: diagnose one injected hang from per-rank dumps, naming the first-cause rank and the victim ranks.
units.stopWhen: You can arm the recorder variables from memory and read a desync plus `fr_trace` output down to the first-cause rank.

fit.note: Both Flight Recorder generations plus the Stas desync and transport sections cover concepts and dump reading; hang diagnosis practice sits in the mini-project.

study.title: Overlap math and roofline tables
study.locator: Communication-Computation Overlap with the overlap inequality and the 7B worked step, and The Memory Wall and Roofline Diagnosis with the intensity table

study.title: Overlap in practice
study.locator: Chapter 4, Overlapping Communication and Computation (Pipelining), with Achieving Maximal Overlap in Practice and Distributed Data Parallel Strategies

focus: Intensity is \(I = \text{FLOPs} / \text{bytes}\). Above the ridge (near 295 FLOP per byte for H100 FP16) the op is compute bound; below it, memory bound. Communication bound means exposed collective time dominates the step.
Exposed communication is total collective time minus the overlapped part. Overlap needs asynchronous buckets or prefetch on separate streams plus enough compute to hide the transfer.
Small messages are launch bound, not bandwidth bound. Doubling bytes halves the bandwidth term but leaves the latency term, so the factor-of-two slogans fail there.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, compute intensity for the JAX Q1 case (about 17M bytes, about 1.07G FLOPs, \(I \approx 63\)) and label it memory bound against a ridge of 295. Then state the exposed-communication formula as total minus overlapped time.
traps: Claiming overlap from asynchronous issue alone. Concurrency needs timeline proof that compute and communication actually coincide.
Quoting reduce-scatter as twice as fast as all-reduce without regime. The factor holds for equal payload in the bandwidth-bound limit only.
Treating intensity as a hardware constant. It is a property of the op shape and batch; the ridge is the hardware property.

selfTest.q: Intensity 63 against ridge 295: which bound?
selfTest.a: Memory bound. Achievable throughput is bandwidth times intensity, well below peak FLOPs.

selfTest.q: What is exposed communication?
selfTest.a: Collective time not hidden under compute: total communication minus the overlapped portion, measured from aligned timelines.

selfTest.q: How do you prove overlap instead of mere asynchrony?
selfTest.a: Show concurrent compute and communication intervals on aligned rank timelines with dependencies that permit concurrency, not just nonblocking calls.

selfTest.q: When does the reduce-scatter factor-of-two claim break?
selfTest.a: For small latency-bound messages and across different algorithms or fabrics. It moves about half the bytes of an equal-payload all-reduce only in the bandwidth-bound limit.

study.locator: DataLoader section with `num_workers`, pinned memory and `non_blocking` device copy, plus the `num-workers-bench.py` and `pin-memory-non-block-bench.py` results

study.title: Storage benchmarking for training
study.locator: Benchmarks section with `fio` for throughput, IOPS and latency, and DLIO for the training-like I/O pattern without accelerators

focus: With `num_workers=0` the accelerator blocks on fetch and transforms. Sweep workers and watch iteration time plus CPU saturation; two workers often suffice and more can hang dual loaders.
`pin_memory=True` with `non_blocking=True` plus prefetch hides host-to-device transfer. Measure with and without; pinned memory alone without async copy buys little.
Sequential versus random reads, local NVMe versus shared filesystem, and preprocessing on CPU versus GPU are different limits. `fio` tests the device; DLIO tests the training pattern.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, sweep `num_workers` from 0 to 4 on a synthetic transform-bound loader, plot mean iteration time with `pin_memory` on and off, and name the count where the curve flattens with CPU saturation as evidence.
traps: Adding workers until the problem disappears. Dual-loader hangs and diminishing returns need a measured optimum, not a maximum.
Setting `pin_memory=True` without `non_blocking=True`. Pinned staging without asynchronous copy still blocks the transfer.
Blaming the interconnect for storage starvation. A slow filesystem or random-read pattern starves every rank identically.

selfTest.q: Iteration time falls from 5.4 s to 0.8 s as workers go 0 to 3, then stalls. What do you conclude?
selfTest.a: Input was the bound up to 3 workers, then compute or another stage dominates. Adding a fourth worker buys nothing; confirm with CPU saturation and trace attribution.

selfTest.q: Why pair `pin_memory` with `non_blocking`?
selfTest.a: Pinned memory enables DMA while nonblocking copy lets the transfer overlap compute. Either alone leaves most of the transfer exposed.

selfTest.q: When does `fio` mislead about training input?
selfTest.a: When the pattern differs: `fio` reports device throughput and IOPS, while training does small random reads with preprocessing. DLIO emulates the loader pattern.

Detect graph breaks and recompilation storms from logs and explain which change triggered them.
units.why: Out-of-memory and sudden slowdowns after a code edit are usually allocator state or compiler guards, not model size. This unit reads the evidence instead of shrinking the batch blindly.

next.note: Check launch gaps once memory is stable.
Separate memory fixes from numerical effects of precision or offload changes.

study.title: CUDA allocator, checkpointing and offload
study.locator: Chapter 13, Profiling and Tuning Memory in PyTorch, with Tuning the CUDA Memory Allocator, Activation Checkpointing for Memory Savings, and Offloading Parameters to CPU and NVMe

study.title: Graph breaks and recompilations
study.locator: Chapter 14, Explaining and Minimizing Graph Breaks, with Graph Breaks and TorchDynamo explain(), Minimize Graph Recompilations, and Debugging Compiler Phases, Graph Breaks, and Performance

study.title: OOM triage and fragmentation fixes
study.locator: Debugging CUDA OOM in forward and backward, Overcoming CUDA OOM due to memory fragmentation with expandable segments, and the memory profiler plus allocation tracing sections

focus: Free memory with no large-enough block is fragmentation; a spike at a known layer is an activation peak; growth across steps is a leak. `torch.cuda.memory_stats` plus the snapshot timeline separates the three.

Fix in order: reserve exact behavior first, then allocator settings, then activation checkpointing or offload. Each change keeps an equivalence check so memory savings do not silently change numerics.
`torch._dynamo.explain` plus `TORCH_LOGS` with graph breaks and recompiles names the break. Dynamic shapes and data-dependent branches add guards; each new guard shape recompiles.
units.reproduce: Without notes, enable the memory snapshot around one training step, capture the peak segment, and explain from the timeline whether the peak is parameters, activations or temporaries. Then run `torch._dynamo.explain` on a toy function with a data-dependent branch and name the break.
traps: Shrinking the batch for a fragmentation OOM. Smaller tensors can fragment worse; expandable segments or staged allocation often fixes the real cause.
Enabling checkpointing without accounting for the extra forward FLOPs. HFU rises while MFU stays flat, and step time changes for a known reason.
Allowing `allow_in_graph` as a quick fix for every break. It bypasses safety checks and can silently produce wrong results.

selfTest.q: Memory shows 10 GB free but a 2 GB allocation fails. What is the likely cause?
selfTest.a: Fragmentation: no single free block fits 2 GB. Check the block-size histogram and expandable-segments behavior before changing the model.

selfTest.q: Peak memory lands on activations at long sequence. Which fixes preserve the update?
selfTest.a: Activation checkpointing with recomputation, or offload with correct restore. Both keep the mathematical update while trading compute or transfer for memory.

selfTest.q: Step time jumps after adding a print of a tensor value. What happened?
selfTest.a: A graph break from data-dependent control flow, likely followed by recompilations per shape. Confirm with explain output and guard counts.

units.title: Kernel launch gaps and rank and node straggler localization
outcomes: Detect kernel launch gaps and small-operation overhead from kernel counts and non-matmul fractions.
Localize a rank or node straggler by elimination with per-rank timings.
Apply graphs or fusion only after traces identify launch overhead as the dominant cost.
units.why: Thousands of tiny launches leave the accelerator idle between kernels, and one slow rank holds every barrier. Both look like low throughput until per-rank timelines separate them.

next.note: Check placement and topology once stragglers are localized.
Turn straggler evidence into health checks and runbooks.

study.title: CUDA graphs for launch overhead
study.locator: Chapter 13, Reducing Kernel Launch Overhead with CUDA Graphs, with Capturing a CUDA Graph and Preallocating Memory and Best Practices for CUDA Graphs

study.title: Straggler detection and mitigation
study.locator: arXiv:2402.15627v1, Section 5: straggler detection, mitigation and diagnosis tooling with measured MFU attached

study.title: Kernel census from traces
study.locator: Section 2.1.4 `nsys_profile` in the Spring 2026 handout: top CUDA kernels, non-matmul share and the AdamW matmul fraction

study.title: Gray stragglers at fleet scale
study.locator: Measurement at Scale with tiered canaries and gray straggler detection, and System Profiling with bottleneck patterns

focus: Launch gaps show as many short kernels with CPU time between them and a high non-matmul share. Small payloads are launch bound: a 5 microsecond launch dwarfs a 36 nanosecond transfer.
Localize stragglers with per-rank step times and barrier waits, then eliminate by node subset. Report max versus median, never the mean alone.
`torch.cuda.CUDAGraph` replay removes Python and launch gaps for static shapes. It is the fix only when the trace already proves launch dominates.
units.reproduce: Without notes, take one profiler trace and compute the top kernel by time, the non-matmul time share, and max versus median rank step time. State launch-bound, kernel-bound or straggler-bound with the numbers.
traps: Fusing kernels before traces identify launch as dominant. Kernel work without a measured launch bottleneck adds complexity for no step-time gain.
Averaging rank times. One slow rank hides inside a healthy mean; max versus median exposes it.
Calling a barrier waiter slow. The waiter is the victim of the straggler that arrives last.

selfTest.q: What trace signature says launch-bound?
selfTest.a: High kernel count with short mean duration, visible CPU gaps between launches, and a large non-matmul time share.

selfTest.q: Ranks report steps of 100, 102, 99 and 250 ms. What do you report?
selfTest.a: A straggler on the fourth rank: median about 101 ms, max 250 ms. The mean hides it; investigate that rank or node first.

selfTest.q: When do CUDA graphs help, and what breaks them?
selfTest.a: They help when launch overhead dominates at static shapes. Dynamic shapes, data-dependent control flow and host syncs break capture or force recapture.

practice.name: CS336 Assignment 2: `nsys_profile` kernel census
practice.locator: Section 2.1.4 `nsys_profile` in the Spring 2026 handout; report the top kernels, the non-matmul share and whether launch or kernels dominate
practice.note: Nsight needs NVIDIA tooling. On CPU use the PyTorch profiler kernel list as the portable substitute and state the substitution.

units.stopWhen: Your trace census names launch, kernel or straggler as the dominant cost with per-rank max versus median evidence.

fit.note: AISys gives the graphs fix, MegaScale and MLSys give straggler method, and CS336 gives the kernel-census practice.

units.title: Network, topology and placement regressions and numerical instability at scale
outcomes: Explain how placement across slow links produces a throughput regression at fixed workload.
Detect a topology or placement regression from bandwidth and trace evidence.
Detect numerical instability from a precision or scale change with equivalence tests.
units.why: A slower step after a move or a dtype switch is two different failures. Placement changes the interconnect; precision changes the arithmetic. Each needs its own test.

next.note: Fix placement policy so compact allocations win.
Turn regression checks into canaries and runbooks.

study.title: Topology, NCCL and multinode pitfalls
study.locator: Chapter 2, Ultrascale Networking with NVLink and NVSwitch, and Chapter 4, Topology Awareness in NCCL with Multinode Communication Pitfalls

study.title: NCCL transport diagnosis
study.locator: How to diagnose NCCL connectivity issues with `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO`, interface selection via `NCCL_IB_HCA` and `NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME`, and `NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS` for collective versus topology failures

study.title: Topology-aware placement
study.locator: Topology-Aware Scheduling with link tiers, compact pod placement and quarantine of limping switches

study.title: Numerical correctness under precision change
study.locator: Chapter 14, Debugging Numerical Correctness and Accuracy, with performance hints and generated-code checks

focus: Moving collectives from NVLink to inter-node links cuts effective bandwidth severalfold. A scattered allocation or a degraded switch shows as stretched communication on traces with unchanged compute.
Read bus bandwidth for the fabric and algorithm bandwidth for the workload. A busbw drop is the network; a stable busbw with slower steps is placement or overlap loss.

Precision switches change range and rounding: FP16 overflows where BF16 survives, and larger scales reorder reductions. Gate every switch on loss and gradient equivalence within a derived tolerance plus overflow counters.
units.reproduce: Without notes, state the two-check procedure for a slower step after a move or dtype switch: first the topology check with `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO` interface and topology lines plus busbw, then the numerical check with reference loss and gradient comparison plus overflow counts.
traps: Quoting microbenchmark busbw as a training speedup. The benchmark measures the fabric; the workload adds overlap, imbalance and launch effects.
Blaming code for a fabric change. A new allocation, a replaced switch or a degraded link regresses throughput with identical code.
Treating BF16 as a wider FP16. Subnormal handling, overflow thresholds and loss-scaling needs differ, so FP16 recipes do not transfer verbatim.

selfTest.q: Steps slow 20 percent with identical code and config. What do you check first?
selfTest.a: Placement and fabric: allocation map, `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO` transport lines, busbw versus history, and whether collectives crossed to slower links.

selfTest.q: Busbw is stable but steps are slower. What does that separate?
selfTest.a: Fabric health from workload placement and overlap. The links deliver, but collectives now cross slower tiers or hide less under compute.

selfTest.q: What gates a precision switch?
selfTest.a: Loss and gradient equivalence against the reference within a derived tolerance, plus overflow and underflow counters, all at fixed workload and seed.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: a placement-regression experiment with busbw and trace evidence, plus a precision-switch equivalence gate with overflow counts.
units.stopWhen: You can separate a placement regression from a numerical regression on one slowed run, with the fabric and equivalence evidence named.

fit.note: AISys gives topology and numerical sections, Stas gives the NCCL transport workflow, and MLSys gives placement policy; experiment practice sits in the mini-project.

units.title: Gang scheduling, quotas, preemption, capacity and Kubernetes versus Slurm
outcomes: Explain gang scheduling and topology-aware placement for synchronous training jobs.
Use quotas, fairness, backfill and preemption vocabulary to predict queue and share behavior.
Compare Kubernetes and Slurm policy controls for one training job.
Explain capacity, queue time and accelerator fragmentation.
units.why: A fast plan that never gets compact accelerators together finishes later than a slower plan that does. Scheduling decides which evidence the fleet can even produce.

next.note: Operate the scheduled fleet with health checks and runbooks.
Convert capacity and queue waste into cost.

study.title: The scheduling problem and paradigms
study.locator: The Scheduling Problem with gang scheduling and fragmentation, and Orchestration Paradigms with Slurm batch versus Kubernetes reconciliation plus Volcano and Kueue

study.title: Placement, elasticity and tenancy
study.locator: Topology-Aware Scheduling with compact placement, Elastic Scheduling with grow-shrink contracts, and Multi-Tenancy and Quotas with fair-share, borrowing and preemption

study.title: Slurm user controls
study.locator: Partitions with `sinfo` and `scontrol`, wait time with `squeue`, allocation and faulty-node exclusion, plus FairShare with `sshare`

study.title: Kubernetes versus Slurm for GPUs
study.locator: Chapter 3, Job Scheduling with Kubernetes and SLURM, with Kubernetes Topology Manager and Slicing a GPU with MIG

focus: Synchronous collectives barrier across ranks, so a training job needs all its accelerators together or none. Fragmentation is idle GPUs that no queued shape fits; topology-aware placement keeps collectives on fast tiers.
Quotas cap shares, fair-share favors historically under-served teams, backfill slides small jobs into idle holes, and preemption reclaims with a checkpoint-and-restart cost.

Slurm speaks partitions, jobs and FairShare. Kubernetes speaks queues, priorities and reconcilers with gang and topology plugins. Both need the same two guarantees: all-or-nothing start and compact placement.
units.reproduce: Without notes, state the gang condition for a synchronous job with \(p\) ranks, give one fragmentation example where free GPUs cannot fit the next queued shape, and name the Slurm and Kubernetes control that expresses each of quota, priority and topology.
traps: Demanding gang scheduling for everything. Asynchronous shards and elastic jobs can grow or shrink; only synchronous barriers need all-or-nothing.
Reading fair-share as an equal split now. It weights history, so a recently heavy team waits behind a light one at equal quotas.
Scheduling without topology. Scattered ranks across slow tiers run measurably slower at identical GPU count.

selfTest.q: Why does synchronous data-parallel training need gang scheduling?
selfTest.a: Every step barriers across ranks in collectives. A partially started job holds accelerators while waiting for the rest, wasting the held share.

selfTest.q: Eight GPUs are free as four plus four on two nodes but the queue wants eight compact. What is this?
selfTest.a: Fragmentation with a topology constraint. The GPUs are idle yet unusable for the queued shape without crossing the slower tier.

selfTest.q: How do backfill and preemption differ in cost?
selfTest.a: Backfill uses idle holes without disturbing running jobs. Preemption reclaims running capacity and pays checkpoint, lost-work and restart costs.

selfTest.q: Which controls set quota and topology in Slurm versus Kubernetes?
selfTest.a: Slurm uses partitions, QoS and FairShare with node constraints and exclusions. Kubernetes uses Queue, PriorityClass and Topology Manager with gang plugins.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: a fleet and placement simulator with gang, topology, quota, fairness, fragmentation, preemption and failure scenarios.
units.stopWhen: You can predict queue, share and placement outcomes for one job under stated quotas and topology, and name the control that enforces each.

fit.note: MLSys covers scheduling through quotas, Stas covers Slurm controls, and AISys covers the Kubernetes comparison; simulator practice sits in the mini-project.

units.title: Health checks, canaries, rollback, runbooks and fleet anomaly detection
outcomes: Design health checks, canaries and rollback gates for a training fleet.
Write a runbook that maps symptom to evidence to cause for hangs, OOMs and stragglers.
Explain fleet anomaly detection over telemetry including gray slow failures.
units.why: Fleets fail in the same few ways. Checks that match those modes plus a rehearsed runbook turn incidents into routine requeues.

next.note: Price the failures the runbook prevents.
Contribute one operated improvement with rollback evidence.

study.title: Debugging utilization and fleet telemetry
study.locator: Debugging Cluster Utilization with policy-topology mismatch diagnosis, and Cost Optimization with spot and checkpoint-on-preemption strategy

study.title: Canaries and gray failures at scale
study.locator: Measurement at Scale with fleet MFU, scaling tax, tiered canaries and gray straggler detection

study.title: Heartbeat, diagnosis and fast restart
study.locator: arXiv:2402.15627v1, Section 4: heartbeat-based detection, automated fault localization and fast recovery

study.title: Faulty-node triage in Slurm
study.locator: Find faulty nodes and exclude them, with the GPU memory check, the NCCL barrier test and the network failure exclusion pattern

focus: Health checks must match the failure taxonomy: GPU access, link errors, memory, plus an NCCL barrier test for collective hangs. Run them at alloc and re-run after any hang before requeue.
A canary is a small fixed workload that must pass before and after each change. Rollback returns to the last-known-good config and checkpoint when it fails.
Gray failures are slow, not dead: limping links, throttled clocks, skewed input. Tiered canaries plus MFU and scaling-tax trends catch what binary alive checks miss.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, write a one-page NCCL-hang runbook: symptom, evidence commands with `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO`, the desync report and `fr_trace` plus per-rank times, a cause table, and actions for exclude, rollback and requeue.
traps: Health checks without a collective test. GPUs can pass memory checks yet hang every all-reduce on a broken link.
Canaries without a fixed workload. An unpinned canary passes or fails for workload reasons, hiding the regression.
Auto-restart onto the same nodes. Without exclusion the job repeats the failure and burns goodput.

selfTest.q: What belongs in a pre-flight health check?
selfTest.a: GPU access and memory, link error counters, interface selection, a small NCCL barrier or all-reduce, and storage reachability. Each maps to a known failure mode.

selfTest.q: How do canary and rollback work together?
selfTest.a: The canary gates promotion: it must pass on the new config. On failure, rollback restores the last-known-good code, config and checkpoint.

selfTest.q: What is a gray failure and what catches it?
selfTest.a: A component that is slow rather than dead, such as a degraded link. Trend canaries, per-rank timing skew and MFU drops catch it; alive checks do not.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: health checks, a canary with rollback, and a runbook rehearsed against an injected hang, OOM and straggler.
units.stopWhen: Your runbook resolves one injected failure to exclusion plus rollback plus requeue, with the evidence trail attached.

fit.note: MLSys gives canary and gray-failure method, MegaScale gives the heartbeat-to-restart loop, and Stas gives node-triage practice; rehearsal sits in the mini-project.

units.title: Cost per useful token and performance per watt
outcomes: Derive cost per useful token from goodput, price and overhead.
Compare throughput and latency designs in cost terms at fixed quality.
Explain performance per watt and where power dominates cost.
units.why: Throughput without price picks pretty configurations. Cost per useful token picks the one the budget can actually train on.

next.note: Justify the contribution in cost per useful token.
Carry cost versus latency tradeoffs into serving design.

study.title: Fleet cost optimization
study.locator: Cost Optimization with idle-cost math, spot versus reserved tiers and checkpoint-on-preemption strategy

study.title: Goodput, power and upgrade ROI
study.locator: Chapter 1, Measuring Goodput Useful Throughput, and Chapter 2, Compute Density and Power Requirements with ROI of Upgrading Your Hardware

study.title: End-to-end time and cost estimate
study.locator: The LLaMA 70B case study with the training time estimate worked from the parallelism plan (44 days at 40 percent MFU)

focus: Cost per useful token is price per hour divided by goodput tokens per hour: \(C = P / G\). Goodput, not raw throughput, belongs in the denominator because failures and idle raise cost per finished token.

Throughput designs with large batches and quantization minimize dollars per token at higher latency. Latency designs with batch one at high precision minimize delay at far higher dollars per token. Fix quality before comparing.
Performance per watt is useful tokens per joule, or \(\text{tokens/s} / \text{watts}\). Idle and cooling watts count; an allocated but stalled fleet still bills and burns.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive dollars per 1k tokens for \(P = 16\) dollars per hour at \(G = 10{,}000\) tokens/s: hourly tokens are \(36{,}000{,}000\), so \(C \approx 4.44 \times 10^{-7}\) dollars per token, about 0.00044 dollars per 1k and 0.44 dollars per 1M.
traps: Pricing raw throughput instead of goodput. Restarts, retries and queue idle are paid for but produce no finished tokens.
Comparing quantized and full-precision dollars per token without a quality gate. Cheaper tokens that break convergence are not cheaper training.
Counting only compute watts. Idle draw, cooling and stalled-but-allocated hours dominate at fleet scale.

selfTest.q: Write the cost-per-useful-token formula and name each term.
selfTest.a: \(C = P / G\) with \(P\) the all-in price per hour and \(G\) the goodput in finished tokens per hour, including failure and idle effects.

selfTest.q: Why can the cheapest dollars-per-token config be the wrong choice?
selfTest.a: It may miss the latency, quality or deadline constraint. Cost compares only among configs that meet quality and schedule gates.

selfTest.q: How does spot pricing change the math?
selfTest.a: Spot lowers \(P\) but adds preemption tax in \(G\): checkpoint, lost work and restart. The switch wins only when the price cut exceeds the goodput cut.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: validate a capacity and cost model for one scenario and explain the residual and portability limits.
units.stopWhen: You can derive dollars per useful token for one scenario from stated price and goodput, and name which overhead dominates it.

fit.note: MLSys gives fleet cost math, AISys gives goodput and power method, and JAX gives a worked end-to-end estimate; model validation sits in the mini-project.

units.title: A small real-code contribution with before and after evidence
outcomes: Instrument a real training codebase with correlated rank, collective and memory timelines for one bottleneck.
Implement one bounded optimization or observability contribution with regression, equivalence and fallback tests.
Compare off versus on under fixed workload with variance, preserving a regime where the change loses or does not apply.
units.why: The section ends where the track ends: a real change to real code, defended by measurement instead of adjectives. Bounded scope plus fallback keeps the contribution reviewable.

next.note: Extend measurement to kernel counters and replay where traces point at kernels.
Carry fixed-workload and cost discipline into serving work.

study.title: Debugging workflow and fake backends
study.locator: Enable Memory Profiling, Fake Backend Debugging with fake versus real-PP-fake-SPMD modes, Memory debugging workflow, and Troubleshooting jobs that timeout with Flight Recorder dumps

study.title: CPU unit tests as the contribution gate
study.locator: `test_checkpoint.py`, `test_fsdp.py` and `test_parallelism_config.py`; run with pytest and keep the suite green before and after the change

study.title: Contribution and measurement requirements
study.locator: Milestone C for hypothesis, invariants, alternatives and reversal conditions, and Milestone E for baseline-versus-alternative comparison with retained negative results

study.title: Ordered optimization method
study.locator: The Optimization Playbook: A 70B LLM Case Study with the diagnostic sequence, combining rules and lessons

focus: Bounded means one measured bottleneck, one seam, one config flag with fallback. Name the hypothesis, the invariants, the predicted regimes and the reversal conditions before coding.

Off-versus-on runs share model, data, batch, precision, topology and correctness oracle, and report step time, tokens/s, memory, communication, utilization and failures with variance. Keep a losing regime in the report.
Defend against two alternatives and show the change addresses the traced critical path rather than an attractive proxy. No benchmark-only special cases and no transfer claims beyond measured scope.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, state the contribution contract: hypothesis, invariants, predicted regimes, two alternatives, reversal conditions, equivalence tests, fallback flag, and the off-versus-on metric set with variance.
traps: Optimizing a microbenchmark instead of the traced critical path. Busbw wins that do not move step time are proxies.
Shipping without fallback or with a benchmark-only branch. The capstone rejects both: retain the baseline path and fail cleanly.
Claiming transfer to other hardware or scales. One GPU plus CPU evidence never proves multi-GPU or multi-node behavior.

selfTest.q: What makes a contribution bounded?
selfTest.a: One bottleneck from a trace, one seam, one flag with fallback, plus stated regimes and reversal conditions. Anything larger is a rewrite, not a contribution.

selfTest.q: What does a complete off-versus-on comparison include?
selfTest.a: Fixed workload and oracle, step time and tokens/s with variance, memory, communication and utilization deltas, failure counts, and a preserved losing or not-applicable regime.

selfTest.q: Why two alternatives?
selfTest.a: They test whether the chosen fix beats the next-best options on the same evidence. A lone proposal cannot show it addresses the bottleneck rather than coinciding with noise.

practice.name: TorchTitan CPU unit tests with one bounded change
practice.locator: Run `test_checkpoint.py`, `test_fsdp.py` and `test_parallelism_config.py` with pytest at the pinned commit, then implement one bounded improvement through the `debugging.md` workflow with fallback and equivalence tests
practice.note: One checkpoint test needs the optional grain package and fails without it; that failure is environmental. Do not attempt a wholesale rewrite.

units.stopWhen: Your change passes the CPU suite, beats the baseline on the traced bottleneck at fixed workload with variance, keeps fallback, and names where it loses or does not transfer.

fit.note: TorchTitan gives the debugging workflow and graded CPU gate, the capstone gives contribution requirements, and MLSys gives the ordered method.
